# The Strength Behind the Team: Five Lessons from ATTR-CM Caregiver Kari Shaw


*As her husband Pete, a former professional football player, navigates life with ATTR-CM, Kari shares what their journey has taught her about love, advocacy, teamwork and the importance of showing up for one another. Learn more about Pete and Kari’s story and ATTR-CM at ATTRGamePlan.com.*


November 13, 2026


Today, as Pete navigates life with hereditary transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (hATTR-CM),1 a serious and often underdiagnosed heart condition, teamwork has taken on a different meaning—one that extends far beyond the football field.


For his wife, Kari, supporting Pete has brought new lessons about recognizing changes in a loved one’s health, finding the confidence to speak up and remembering that caregivers need support, too.


Like many caregivers, Kari never expected to take on this role. But through the questions, uncertainty and adjustments that come with a serious diagnosis,1-3 she’s learned that caregiving isn’t about having all the answers. It’s about facing the unknown together.


Here, Kari shares five lessons from her experience that she hopes will resonate with others supporting someone they love.


## **1. Trust what you notice**


Pete spent years playing professional football, where pushing through physical challenges was part of the job. But when changes in his health began to emerge, understanding what was happening wasn’t always straightforward.


For Kari, knowing Pete so well gave her a perspective that was important in recognizing when something seemed different.


“When you love someone, you notice the things other people might miss. Pete spent years as a professional athlete, pushing through whatever came his way, so it was easy to think some of the changes we were seeing were just part of getting older.2 Looking back, I’ve learned how important it is to trust what you notice, even when those changes seem small. Sometimes, those little things are worth a much bigger conversation.”2


For caregivers, paying attention to changes in a loved one’s health, and feeling empowered to speak up about them, can be an important first step toward getting answers.


## ****2. Don’t be afraid to ask questions****


Navigating a diagnosis like ATTR-CM can mean learning an entirely new language of medical terms while managing appointments, decisions and a constant flow of new information.2,4


For Kari, one of the most important lessons has been recognizing that advocacy doesn’t require having all the answers. Sometimes, it starts with simply asking another question.


“When we first heard the word amyloidosis, I remember thinking, ‘amyloidosis? Ama-what?’ We could barely pronounce it, let alone understand what it meant. Suddenly, we were trying to make sense of a diagnosis we’d never heard of, and it was overwhelming.4 But I’ve learned that you don’t have to understand everything right away. Sometimes, the most important thing you can do is ask another question, speak up when something doesn’t make sense and keep asking until you feel informed. You don’t have to be a medical expert to be an advocate for someone you love.”


By asking questions, sharing observations and staying engaged in conversations with Pete’s care team, Kari has found ways to support her husband while ensuring they both feel informed and heard.


## ******3. Remember, you’re on the same team******


************


For a former professional athlete like Pete, the value of teamwork is familiar. But as Kari has learned, being a teammate in caregiving looks different from being one on the football field.


It’s not about taking over or making every decision. It’s about understanding how to support each other while continuing to move forward as partners.


“Pete knows what it means to have a team behind him. But I’ve learned that being his teammate in this chapter of our lives isn’t about taking the lead or having all the answers. It’s about knowing when to speak up, when to listen and when to simply stand beside him. Football may have taught Pete the value of teamwork, but this experience has given that word a whole new meaning for both of us.”


For Kari and Pete, that shared approach has become an important part of navigating life with ATTR-CM – recognizing that while their roles may evolve, they are still facing life’s challenges side by side.


## **4. Make room for yourself, too**


When someone you love is managing a serious health condition, it’s natural to focus on their needs. But amid the appointments, questions and day-to-day responsibilities, caregivers can sometimes lose sight of their own well-being.4


Kari has learned that being there for Pete doesn’t mean she has to carry every worry or responsibility on her own.


“When someone you love is going through something difficult, it’s easy to put your own feelings aside.4 You tell yourself that they’re the one facing the diagnosis, so you need to be strong. But I’ve learned that being strong doesn’t mean doing everything on your own. It’s okay to have hard days, to ask for help and to admit that you need support, too. Taking care of yourself doesn’t mean you’re showing up any less for the person you love.”


For Kari, making room for her own needs isn’t separate from caregiving. It’s part of finding a way to support Pete while recognizing that her well-being matters, too.


## ****5. You don’t have to get it all right****


Perhaps one of the most meaningful lessons Kari has learned is that there is no perfect roadmap for caregiving.


There will be moments of uncertainty, difficult conversations and days when the next step isn’t clear.2 But caregiving isn’t measured by having every answer or making every decision perfectly.


“If there’s one thing I would tell another caregiver, it’s that you don’t have to get everything right. There will be days when you don’t have the answers, when you’re worried or when you wonder if you’re doing enough. I’ve learned that what matters most isn’t being perfect. It’s continuing to show up for each other, even on the hard days. Pete and I may not know exactly what every day will bring, but we know we’re facing it together.”


For Kari and Pete, navigating ATTR-CM has reinforced something they’ve always believed: no one should face life’s challenges alone.


While every caregiving experience is different, Kari hopes her story encourages others to trust what they notice, find their voice and recognize the difference they can make in the lives of those they love.


And just as importantly, she hopes caregivers remember that they deserve support, too.
